summary: The sanctuary's structure is specified through joined linen curtains, a larger goats' hair covering, outer skins, and an upright wooden frame with sockets and bars. An inner veil separates the ark from the table and lamp stand, while a distinct embroidered screen forms the tent's entrance.
whyItMatters: The design makes a single portable dwelling out of many fitted parts and creates distinct spaces within it. Attention to the different coverings and partitions helps the reader understand later movement toward and within the sanctuary.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The mountain instructions to Moses for the enclosure that will contain the sanctuary furnishings.
context.literaryForm: Sequential building specifications moving from fabric coverings to supporting frame and interior partitions.

before.text: The ark, its cover, the table, and the lamp stand have been specified. Their positions now become part of the plan for the tent that will house them.

here.text: Keep the joined coverings, supporting frame, inner veil, and outer screen distinct; the chapter gives each different materials or structural duties.

after.text: The following instructions move outside to the bronze altar and the surrounding court, then assign the priests the maintenance of the light.

outline.heading: Ten joined linen curtains
outline.note: Two groups of five decorated curtains become one unit through loops and gold clasps.

outline.heading: The larger tent covering and skins
outline.note: Eleven goats’ hair curtains overlap the inner structure and receive additional outer coverings.

outline.heading: Boards and silver sockets
outline.note: Upright acacia boards and their bases form the sides and rear corners.

outline.heading: Bars and the mountain pattern
outline.note: Gold-covered bars join the frame, which must follow the shown arrangement.

outline.heading: The inner veil and placement of furniture
outline.note: The veil separates the most holy place from the table and lamp stand.

outline.heading: The entrance screen
outline.note: A different hanging and five bronze-based pillars mark the tent’s doorway.

keyVerses.text: You shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains to one another with the clasps. The tabernacle shall be a unit.
keyVerses.why: The joining devices serve the stated aim that the tabernacle be one unit.

keyVerses.text: You shall hang up the veil under the clasps, and shall bring the ark of the covenant in there within the veil. The veil shall separate the holy place from the most holy for you.
keyVerses.why: The veil creates the chapter’s decisive division between holy and most holy space.

keyVerses.text: You shall set the table outside the veil, and the lamp stand opposite the table on the side of the tabernacle toward the south. You shall put the table on the north side.
keyVerses.why: The table and lamp stand receive precise relative positions outside the inner veil.

questions.question: Why distinguish ten curtains from eleven curtains?
questions.answer: The ten linen curtains with cherubim form one joined inner unit, while the eleven goats' hair curtains form a larger covering above it. The extra material folds at the front and hangs beyond the inner structure, so these are different layers rather than contradictory counts of the same set.

questions.question: How are the two curtain systems joined?
questions.answer: Each uses opposite loops and fifty clasps, but the inner linen system has gold clasps and the goats' hair system bronze. The repeated joining instructions explain how separate panels become a continuous enclosure.

questions.question: What are “tenons” in the frame?
questions.answer: They are the paired projecting joins on each board that fit with the supporting sockets described immediately afterward. The term names a structural connection between the upright boards and their bases.

questions.question: Why can drawings of the sanctuary’s frame differ?
questions.answer: It gives measurements, boards, corners, sockets, and bars while also referring to a pattern shown to Moses. The corner arrangement in particular is compressed, so reconstructions can differ while following the stated measurements.

questions.question: What is kept inside the veil?
questions.answer: The ark of the covenant with its gold cover belongs in the most holy place. The table and lamp stand remain outside that veil, on the north and south sides respectively, giving the internal division a practical relation to the furnishings.

questions.question: Does the veil make every part of the sanctuary interchangeable?
questions.answer: No. Its stated function is to separate the holy place from the most holy, so the design establishes a boundary even within sacred space. The chapter specifies the boundary but does not yet give a complete schedule of who may cross it and when.

questions.question: How is the entrance screen different from the inner veil?
questions.answer: Both use colored material and fine linen, but the inner veil has cherubim and hangs on four pillars with silver sockets. The doorway screen is described as embroidery and uses five pillars with bronze sockets, marking a separate location and structure.

glossary.def: The projecting joins on the upright boards that fit into their supporting bases.
The metal bases that receive the boards or pillars of the structure.
The inner hanging that separates the most holy place from the holy place.
